questions.subject: WEB_DEVELOPMENT
questions.topic: Choosing one representative input per equivalence class of a fee function
questions.learningObjective: identify the equivalence classes of a function and pick a representative for each
questions.practice: choosing representatives for a fee function
questions.stem: A shipping fee is `function fee(weightKg, express) { if (weightKg <= 0) return 'rejected'; if (weightKg > 30) return 'oversize'; return express ? 12 + weightKg * 2 : 5 + weightKg; }`. A writer must choose one representative input per equivalence class, and the set has to include both boundary points. Which candidate set is complete?

options.text: 0 kg plain, 15 kg plain, 15 kg express, 30.5 kg plain: one input per class with both limits covered
0 kg plain, 15 kg plain, 30 kg plain: one input per class, because 15 already stands in for express
options.misconception: believes the plain and express branches form one class because both succeed

options.text: 0 kg plain, 0.1 kg plain, 1 kg plain, 30 kg plain: every edge of the accepted range is represented
options.misconception: believes each value inside one branch is a class of its own

options.text: 15 kg plain, 15 kg express, 30 kg plain, 31 kg plain: the edges of the accepted range are covered
options.misconception: believes the branch that refuses the parcel needs no representative

questions.explanation: The classes are exactly the four the code distinguishes: refused at or below zero, oversize above thirty, accepted plain, and accepted express. Set A holds one input from each, and 0 and 30.5 sit either side of the two limits, so a change that moves either boundary from <= to < is caught. Set B looks complete until you notice the express branch is never entered. Set C tests three values that all take the same path, which is the shape of a test that stays green while the function is wrong, and Set D leaves the refused branch untested, so a fee that accepted a zero weight parcel would pass the suite.
questions.hint: Count the branches the function can take, then check each candidate for one input per branch and for a value on each side of both limits.

questions.subject: WEB_DEVELOPMENT
questions.topic: Tracing a capped percentage discount across its boundary values
questions.learningObjective: trace a discount function across the values around a rounding boundary
questions.stem: A discount is `function discount(subtotal, code) { if (code !== 'SAVE10' && code !== 'SAVE20') return 0; const pct = code === 'SAVE10' ? 10 : 20; return Math.min(Math.round(subtotal * pct / 100), 25); }`. The suite calls it once for each subtotal in [19.99, 20, 24.99, 25, 25.01, 100] with 'SAVE10'. Which list of results does it produce?

options.text: 2, 2, 2, 3, 3, 10, because the cap sits far above every one of these subtotals
2, 2, 2, 3, 3, 25, because the cap of 25 applies to the smaller subtotals
options.misconception: believes the cap is the smaller of the computed value and the percentage

options.text: 1, 2, 2, 2, 3, 10, because the percentage is truncated rather than rounded
options.misconception: believes the fractional part is discarded instead of rounded to nearest

options.text: 2, 2, 2, 2, 3, 10, because a subtotal of exactly 25 rounds down rather than up
options.misconception: believes rounding breaks ties downwards rather than to the nearest value

questions.explanation: Ten percent of each subtotal is 1.999, 2, 2.499, 2.5, 2.501 and 10, and rounding those to nearest gives 2, 2, 2, 3, 3 and 10. The interesting case is 25, where the exact value 2.5 rounds up to 3, so a suite that only tests 24.99 and 25.01 misses the tie. The cap never fires in this run: the computed value has to exceed 25, which needs a subtotal of 245 or more, so a test list chosen around the cap rather than around the rounding boundary would prove nothing about these six values.
questions.hint: Compute ten percent of each subtotal, round each one, and check separately whether the cap can ever be the smaller number here.

questions.subject: WEB_DEVELOPMENT
questions.topic: Reading a statement coverage figure off a tracer
questions.learningObjective: compute line coverage from the statements a suite actually reaches
questions.stem: A tracer records each statement a run reaches: `function finalise(items, options) { hit.add('a'); const list = items.filter(i => !i.void); hit.add('b'); if (options.expedited) { hit.add('c'); return list.map(i => ({ ...i, handling: 15 })); } hit.add('d'); return list.map(i => ({ ...i, handling: 0 })); }`. The suite calls it three times, always with `{ expedited: false }`: once with an empty list, once with a live item, once with a voided item. What does the report show?

options.text: 75 percent, because no call reaches the expedited branch and statement c is never hit
100 percent, because every call enters the function and produces a returned value
options.misconception: believes entering the function is enough to cover the statements inside it

options.text: 50 percent, because the filter and the map each count as a statement of their own
options.misconception: believes a multi-call expression is counted once per call it contains

options.text: 75 percent, because the filter is skipped when the list handed in is empty
options.misconception: believes a filter over an empty array does not run at all

questions.explanation: Running the three calls marks a, b and d, and never c, so three of the four statements are covered and the figure is 75 percent. The empty list is the trap in the distractor: the filter still runs on an empty array and still marks b, so a missing call would be a test that passes without checking anything. This is also the shape of a coverage number worth distrusting: all three calls take the same branch, so the number is high and tells you almost nothing about the expedited path, which is the one that costs money.
questions.hint: Trace the labels each call marks, then divide the marked statements by the total, and check whether the empty-list call still reaches the filter.

questions.subject: WEB_DEVELOPMENT
questions.topic: Counting the branch outcomes a short circuiting suite reaches
questions.learningObjective: count branch outcomes rather than conditions to measure branch coverage
questions.stem: A tracer logs the outcome of every condition it evaluates: `function canShip(order) { hit.add('paid is ' + order.paid); if (!order.paid) return 'block'; hit.add('stock over zero is ' + (order.stock > 0)); if (order.stock <= 0) return 'block'; hit.add('address present is ' + Boolean(order.address)); if (!order.address) return 'hold'; return 'ship'; }`. The suite calls it with {paid:false,stock:5,address:'x'}, then {paid:true,stock:0,address:'x'}, then {paid:true,stock:5,address:'x'}. How many of the six branch outcomes does it take?

options.text: Five of six, because the third call evaluates the address check as true and never as false
Six of six, because the three calls between them exercise each condition both ways
options.misconception: believes three inputs can cover six outcomes when each input is a single path

options.text: Four of six, because the first call stops before the stock check is ever evaluated
options.misconception: believes a condition skipped by short circuiting still counts as covered

options.text: Three of six, because one outcome per condition is counted however many times it repeats
options.misconception: believes repeated outcomes of the same condition do not add to the total

questions.explanation: The three calls mark paid false, paid true, stock false, stock true and address true, which is five of the six possible outcomes, so branch coverage reads 83 percent while line coverage on the same suite reads higher. The missing outcome is the address check coming back false, the only path that returns hold, and no input in the suite produces it. Counting conditions instead of outcomes is the common way to get this number wrong: three conditions are named in the source, but each one has two outcomes and only one of the six is untested.
questions.hint: List the outcome each call records, count the distinct outcomes, and compare that with twice the number of conditions.

questions.subject: WEB_DEVELOPMENT
questions.topic: Shared module state that lets one test change another
questions.learningObjective: trace how a module level value lets tests pass or fail depending on order
questions.stem: A helper exports one array for the whole run: `const cart = { items: [], add(i) { this.items.push(i); return this.items.length; } }`. Test one calls `cart.add('apple')` and asserts the result is 1. Test two calls `cart.add('pear')` and asserts the result is 2. Neither test clears the array. What happens when the file runs in the declared order, and what happens when the runner reverses them?

options.text: Both pass in the declared order, and both fail in the reversed order with lengths 1 and 2
Both pass in either order, because each test pushes exactly one item before asserting
options.misconception: believes the assertion is insulated from whatever ran before it

options.text: Test one passes in both orders, and test two fails only when it runs second
options.misconception: believes a test whose input it creates cannot be affected by a preceding one

options.text: Both fail in the declared order, because the second push makes the count 3 rather than 2
options.misconception: counts one extra push that the code does not perform

questions.explanation: The array is created once when the module loads and lives for the whole file, so the first push leaves length 1 and the second leaves length 2, which is what both assertions expect when they run in order. Reversed, test two runs first, sees length 1 and fails, and test one then sees length 2 and fails. The failure is not about the cart, it is about the runner, and that is what makes this class of failure so expensive: a green suite can be one reorder away from red, and the reorder usually arrives as part of an unrelated change to a different file.
questions.hint: Work out how many times the module is initialised, then run the two calls in the stated order and in the reverse.

questions.subject: WEB_DEVELOPMENT
questions.topic: An expectation computed from the code under test, which cannot fail
questions.learningObjective: recognise a test that compares the code against itself
questions.practice: finding a test that cannot fail
questions.stem: A test builds its own expectation from the function it is meant to check: `function decorate(list) { return list.map(r => ({ ...r, label: r.tags.join(',') + '!' })); } const rows = [{id:1,tags:['a']},{id:2,tags:[]}]; const actual = decorate(rows); const expected = decorate(rows); assert.deepEqual(actual, expected);`. The join is wrong: a label should never end in an exclamation mark. What does this test report?

options.text: It passes, and it would keep passing with any change made to decorate at all
It fails, because the trailing mark makes the two objects different in shape
options.misconception: believes a wrong value inside an object is enough to fail a deep comparison

options.text: It passes now and fails once decorate is corrected, because the fix changes both sides
options.misconception: believes a test that shares its implementation fails when the bug is fixed

options.text: It fails, because rows is mutated by the call and the second call sees a different array
options.misconception: believes a spread copy shares its array elements with the original

questions.explanation: Both sides are produced by the same call on the same input, so they are equal whatever the function does, and the run reports a pass while the labels come out as 'a!' and '!'. A comparison is only evidence when the two sides come from different places, one from the implementation and one written by a person or taken from a specification. This is the shape of a test that can never fail, and it is common precisely because it looks thorough: someone derived the expected value programmatically to avoid typing a large fixture, and in doing so removed the only part of the test that could have disagreed with the code.
questions.hint: Ask where each side of the comparison comes from, and what would have to change for them to differ.

questions.subject: WEB_DEVELOPMENT
questions.topic: A test double that stays reachable once the code is deployed
questions.learningObjective: trace a module level substitution that survives into a production run
questions.stem: Pricing reads through one mutable holder: `const real = { base: 100 }; let impl = real; export function price(qty) { return impl.base * qty; } export function useTestDouble() { impl = { base: 1 }; }`. An analytics module calls `useTestDouble()` during start-up so that a preview environment reports round numbers. Nothing checks which environment it is running in. What does `price(3)` return in production?

options.text: 3, because the holder is module level so the substitution outlives the process that made it
300, because the real implementation is bound when the module is first evaluated
options.misconception: believes a reassignment inside a function cannot outlive the function

options.text: 3 in preview and 300 in production, because the caller is told which environment it is in
options.misconception: believes the environment is passed in even though nothing reads it

options.text: 300, because the analytics module is only loaded when previews are switched on
options.misconception: believes a bundled module is excluded from production builds by default

questions.explanation: The holder lives in the module scope of the pricing module, so the moment useTestDouble runs in the same process, every later call to price reads the substituted object and 3 times a quantity of 1 comes back, in production, with no error and no log line. The fix is not to be careful with the helper, it is to remove the ability to swap the dependency: pass the implementation in as an argument, so a test can supply a double and production cannot. A double that is installed by a code path reachable in production is not a test artefact, it is a latent discount of ninety nine percent.
questions.hint: Ask how long the mutable holder lives and whether anything in the code path decides which environment it is in.

questions.subject: WEB_DEVELOPMENT
questions.topic: A stored snapshot that a harmless edit invalidates
questions.learningObjective: trace what a text comparison of output does and does not notice
questions.stem: A snapshot test stores the text `{"name":"ada","roles":["dev","ops"],"createdAt":"2024-01-01"}` for one user. A refactor rewrites the renderer to emit the three fields in the order createdAt, roles, name, changing no value. A second refactor adds a fourth field, plan, with the value free. Which statement is true of the two refactors?

options.text: The first fails the stored snapshot with identical data, and the second fails it with a real change
Both fail, because a stored text comparison notices any difference in the characters produced
options.misconception: believes a character level comparison is sensitive to meaning

options.text: The first passes, because the values compare equal, and the second fails as it should
options.misconception: believes a stored text comparison compares the values rather than the layout

options.text: Both pass, because the field names and the values in the output are unchanged
options.misconception: believes adding a field leaves a comparison of the previous fields unaffected

questions.explanation: A stored snapshot is a string, so it fails on any difference in the characters and only then on any difference in the data. Reordering the keys changes the characters and not the data, so the refactor is reported as a failure the writer has to read and approve for no reason, and that habit of approving without reading is the real cost. Adding a field is a genuine change, but the snapshot cannot say so, which is why a reviewer learns to treat a red snapshot as routine. The narrow fix is a structural comparison or a normaliser that sorts keys and drops fields nobody is asserting on.
questions.hint: Compare the stored string with each new string, then compare the values the two strings describe once key order is ignored.

questions.subject: WEB_DEVELOPMENT
questions.topic: A generated counterexample and the property it violates
questions.learningObjective: read a generated counterexample and name the property it breaks
questions.stem: A generated case study runs `applyCoupon(items, 'SAVE')`, which discounts whichever item comes first in the list: `function applyCoupon(items, code) { const out = []; let n = 0; for (const it of items) { n += 1; if (code === 'SAVE' && n === 1) out.push({ ...it, price: Math.round(it.price * 90) / 100 }); else out.push(it); } return out; }`. With seed 1234 the first failing case is a list of prices [104, 375, 174]. Which statement about that case is correct?

options.text: The same list totals 642.6 in order and 635.6 reversed, so the discount depends on position
The same list totals 642.6 in both orders, so the case shows only that rounding is in play
options.misconception: believes reversing a list cannot change which item is discounted first

options.text: The reversed total is higher, so the case shows the discount being applied twice to one item
options.misconception: believes the counter shows a larger total after reversing the list

options.text: The case passes a discount that never raises the total, so the property tested is the wrong one
options.misconception: believes a property about the total can detect a discount tied to position

questions.explanation: Discounting the first item of [104, 375, 174] gives 93.6, and 93.6 plus 375 plus 174 is 642.6. Reverse the list and the discount lands on 174, giving 156.6 plus 375 plus 104, which is 635.6. The same basket is therefore worth two different amounts depending on the order the rows arrived in, which is the property that broke: the total after a coupon must not depend on the order of the input. The easier property, that a discount never raises the total, holds across the whole generated run, so a suite built on it alone reports nothing at all.
questions.hint: Apply the discount to the first item of each ordering and add up the three prices both ways.

questions.subject: WEB_DEVELOPMENT
questions.topic: What a recorded seed does and does not make reproducible
questions.learningObjective: explain the role of a seed in reproducing a generated failure
questions.stem: A generated case study records the seed with every failure and prints it in the report, `fail(seed) -> { for (let t = 1; t <= 2000; t += 1) { const list = makeList(lcg(seed)); if (broken(list)) return { trial: t, list }; } return null; }`. Re-running with seed 1234 produces the first failing case at trial 1, the list [104, 375, 174]. Re-running with seed 99 produces its first failing case at trial 1, the list [130, 303]. Which statement follows?

options.text: Each seed reproduces its own case exactly, and changing it explores a different part of the input space
The seed only affects the order cases are reported in, since the same bug is found either way
options.misconception: believes a different seed searches a different set of inputs

options.text: Recording the seed makes the run pass, because the failing input is then known to the generator
options.misconception: believes reproducing a failure removes it from later runs

options.text: Both seeds found a failure at trial 1, so the generator is not really exploring the input space
options.misconception: believes an early first failure means the search is not searching

questions.explanation: The seed fixes the whole sequence of generated inputs, so replaying 1234 gives the identical list and replaying 99 gives a different one, which is exactly what makes a recorded seed worth storing. What the seed does not do is make the property true: the run still fails, and the same bug is found through a different input. That is the point of generating inputs rather than writing them, since the hand-written case is the one already in the author's head, and a record of the seed turns an unreproducible red build into a single command.
questions.hint: Decide what the seed controls, then check whether replaying a seed can change the outcome rather than only the input.

questions.topic: Counting the tests in a file that can fail at all
questions.learningObjective: count the tests in a file that contain an assertion
questions.practice: auditing a test file for assertions
questions.stem: A file declares five tests. 'adds two numbers' asserts 1 + 1 equals 2. 'rejects empty cart' asserts that an empty array has length greater than zero. 'renders a row' calls the renderer and discards the result. 'formats money' asserts (1.5).toFixed(2) equals '1.50'. 'rejects a bad id' asserts Number.isInteger('x'). How many of the five can fail?

options.text: Two, and the other three would still be reported as passing if the code they call were deleted
Four, because a test that calls a function has checked that the call did not throw
options.misconception: believes calling a function is an assertion about what it returned

options.text: Five, because the runner reports a result for every declared test either way
options.misconception: believes a declared test always carries a check of some kind

options.text: Three, because the two arithmetic tests are checked by the runner as well as by the file
options.misconception: believes the runner repeats the assertions the file already makes

questions.explanation: Only the two tests that compare a value with something can fail, and one of those two compares two things that were true before the code under test existed, so in practice the file is guarding very little. The three tests with no assertion pass by construction: a renderer that returned nothing, or returned the wrong element, or threw, changes nothing about the report unless the throw is what fails the run. Counting this way is cheap and catches the most common way a suite grows large and stays empty, which is by adding tests that exercise a path without checking its result.
questions.hint: Ask test by test what value is compared with what, and treat a call with no comparison as unchecked.

questions.topic: A test that pins a wording rather than a behaviour
questions.learningObjective: explain why asserting on a log string couples a test to wording
questions.stem: A function logs before refusing bad input. `function checkAge(age) { if (age < 0) { log('WARN: negative age given: ' + age); return false; } return true; }`. The test asserts the captured line equals 'WARN: negative age given: -1'. A later change rewords the message to 'WARN: age cannot be negative, got: ' plus the value. What does the test do, and what does the function still do?

options.text: The test fails and the function still refuses a negative age, because the return value did not change
The test fails and the function starts accepting negative ages, because the guard moved
options.misconception: believes rewording a message changes which inputs are refused

options.text: The test passes, because the assertion was written on the prefix and the prefix is unchanged
options.misconception: believes an exact string assertion tolerates a changed ending

options.text: The test fails and the caller now sees true, because the log call replaced the return statement
options.misconception: believes a log call returns the value the function needed to return

questions.explanation: The behaviour under test is the refusal, and that is unchanged: both versions return false for a negative age. The assertion was written on the whole line, so the reword trips it, and a developer now has to decide whether a message change deserves to break a build. The logging case is a special kind of this, because the log line is usually written for a person reading a dashboard rather than for a machine, so pinning it in a test makes the wording load bearing. Assert the return value or the state change, and leave the sentence to the people who read it.
questions.hint: Separate the return value from the line the test captured, then change only the wording and see which of them moved.

questions.topic: A file coverage figure assembled from two functions
questions.learningObjective: assemble a file coverage figure from per function counts
questions.stem: A tracer marks a statement each time it runs. `alpha` has three statements a1, a2, a3 and is called once with 1 and once with 0, so all three are marked. `beta` has three statements b1, b2, b3 and is called only with 1, so b1 and b2 are marked. What line coverage figure does the report print for the file, and which function is the one worth looking at?

options.text: 83 percent, and beta is the one to look at, because its unmarked branch is the one nobody called
67 percent, and both functions are equally worth looking at for the same reason
options.misconception: believes two functions with the same ratio hide the same amount

options.text: 83 percent, and alpha is the one to look at, because it is called more often than beta
options.misconception: believes call frequency is what coverage measures

options.text: 100 percent, because the file as a whole was entered by every test that ran
options.misconception: believes per function marking adds up to whole file marking

questions.explanation: Five of the six statements are marked, which is 83 percent, and the single unmarked statement is b3, the one beta takes when it is given a zero. Alpha is fully covered, so the whole gap in the file sits in one branch of one function, which is exactly the kind of thing a percentage hides. The figure is also a reminder that averaging hides concentration: a file at 83 percent can be one function at 100 and another at 67, and the second is where the untested behaviour is.
questions.hint: Count the marked statements across both functions, divide by the total, then look at which function holds the unmarked statement.

questions.topic: A surviving mutant and the assertion that would have killed it
questions.learningObjective: read a mutation score and name the test that would kill the survivor
questions.stem: Under test is `function eligible(u) { return u.age >= 18 && u.verified; }`. The suite has two cases: a 20 year old who is verified must be eligible, and a 17 year old who is verified must not. Three mutants are tried: replacing the conjunction with a disjunction, replacing 18 with 17, and dropping the verified term entirely. Which mutant survives, and what would kill it?

options.text: The dropped term survives, and a 20 year old who is not verified must be ineligible
The disjunction survives, and a 20 year old who is not verified must be ineligible
options.misconception: believes a disjunction still returns false when only one side is true

options.text: The changed constant survives, and a 17 year old who is verified must be ineligible
options.misconception: believes lowering the threshold leaves the existing minor case failing

options.text: All three survive, because both cases in the suite are about the age rather than the flag
options.misconception: believes two cases is enough to kill every change to a conjunction

questions.explanation: The two existing cases both supply verified as true, so removing the term changes nothing they can see and the mutant survives; the mutation score is two killed out of three, and the surviving one is the interesting one. The disjunction and the lowered constant are both caught by the 17 year old case, which is why that case earns its place. A mutation score is a sharper instrument than coverage precisely because it reports the assertions that failed to discriminate, and a survivor is a request for one more case rather than a defect in the code.
questions.hint: Run all three mutants against both cases, then find the input for which the surviving mutant and the original disagree.

questions.topic: A test whose outcome depends on an unseeded generator
questions.learningObjective: explain why an unseeded sample makes a test fail intermittently
questions.stem: A test does `function pick(list) { return list[Math.floor(Math.random() * list.length)]; } assert(pick([1, 2, 3]) < 3);` and it fails on some runs and passes on others. Over three million seeded trials of the same assertion, 998,924 fail. What is the rate, and what is the cause?

options.text: About one run in three, because the sampled index lands on the last element that often
About one run in thirty, because the generator is only consulted on some calls
options.misconception: believes the generator is skipped for part of the samples

options.text: Exactly one run in two, because an index of two is as likely as any other value
options.misconception: believes three elements give two equally likely outcomes

options.text: The rate cannot be stated, because the count depends on the machine the tests run on
options.misconception: believes a probability over three outcomes varies between machines

The code under test is not intermittent; the input is. The fix is to stop asserting on one draw, for example to assert that the result is one of the members, or to seed the generator with a value recorded in the failure so the exact draw can be replayed. A test that depends on chance cannot be debugged from its own output, because the output changes every time.
questions.hint: Divide the seeded failure count by the number of trials, then work out how often one index out of three lands on the value the assertion rejects.

questions.subject: WEB_DEVELOPMENT
questions.topic: Reading a percentile out of a run of recorded latencies
questions.learningObjective: compute a tail percentile and explain what it shows that a mean hides
questions.stem: A load run issues requests through `const samples = Array.from({ length: 200 }, (_, i) => lat[i % lat.length]); const sorted = samples.sort((a, b) => a - b); const pct = (p) => sorted[Math.ceil(p / 100 * sorted.length) - 1];` where `lat` is a fixed list of 20 values, so the run is repeatable. The first run gives mean 80.0 ms, median 40 ms, ninety fifth percentile 260 ms, ninety ninth 400 ms. The same run is then repeated with ten of the calls replaced by 900 ms values. What does the mean become, and what does the ninety fifth percentile become?

options.text: The mean rises to about 118 ms and the ninety fifth percentile goes to 400 ms, so the tail moved and the mean partly followed
The mean stays at 80 ms and the percentile goes to 400 ms, because a mean ignores extreme values
options.misconception: believes a mean is unmoved by any number of large values

options.text: The mean rises to 118 ms and the percentile stays at 260 ms, because the percentile is fixed once chosen
options.misconception: believes a percentile reports the same point however the data changes

options.text: Both figures stay at 80 ms and 260 ms, because a repeatable latency list cannot change
options.misconception: believes cycling a fixed list produces a different distribution when edited

questions.explanation: Replacing ten values of the list with 900 adds 7000 ms to a total of 16000 ms spread over 200 calls, so the mean moves from 80 to about 118. The ninety fifth percentile moves to 400 because the slow calls now occupy the top five percent of the sorted list. Both numbers move, which is the point: a mean can absorb a tail problem for a long time, ten bad calls in two hundred barely dent it, while a percentile taken near the top reports the tail directly. That is why a latency budget is written against a percentile and an alert is set on one.

questions.topic: Two benchmark pairs whose differences mean different things

Candidate A has median 98.45 and a range of 90.33 to 109.62. Candidate A2 has median 101.91 and a range of 92.99 to 112.91. Candidate B has median 142.54 and a range of 126.95 to 153.59. Which comparison is sound?

options.text: B is genuinely slower, because its median is 45 percent above A while either range spans about 19 percent
A2 is genuinely slower than A, because its median is higher by three and a half percent
options.misconception: believes a higher median is a result even when the ranges overlap

options.text: Neither comparison is sound, because a benchmark with jitter can never support a conclusion
options.misconception: believes that any measured difference is smaller than the noise by definition

options.text: A is faster than both, because the lowest single run is the best estimate of each candidate
options.misconception: believes the minimum of a noisy run is the value to compare

Three hits and three real uses, so the job is about to succeed for the right reason

options.misconception: believes a bound reference and a table entry stop the function being called

options.text: Four hits and three real uses, so the job overcounts by one but still finds them all
options.misconception: believes a name built from two strings is matched by a text search

It accepts all three rows and the test has to filter out the negative quantity afterwards

The discount check, because arithmetic is the easiest thing to get wrong and so needs the most testing
options.misconception: believes the most failure prone behaviour belongs in the most expensive layer

options.text: The receipt totals check, because a printed total is the only output a customer ever actually sees

options.misconception: believes the severity of a failure decides which layer should catch it

questions.stem: Three doubles appear in one suite: a logger passed in only so the signature is satisfied, a repository that returns an empty list without consulting anything, and a mailer that records every address it was given. Which description matches them?

A stub, a dummy, and a spy, in that order, each replacing behaviour less than the last
options.misconception: believes the logger substitutes more behaviour than the repository does

options.text: A mock, a stub, and a dummy, in that order, each asserting on more calls than the last
options.misconception: believes the object that records calls substitutes the most behaviour

options.text: Three stubs of equal standing, differing only in whether the replaced thing was ever constructed
options.misconception: believes a placeholder and a recorded collaborator are the same kind of object

questions.stem: A stub returns a fixed list of orders. A mock returns the same list and records every call made to it. The test passes with the stub and passes with the mock. Which statement is true of the difference?

options.text: The stub test would still pass if the code asked for the orders once or four times, and the mock test would not
The mock test is weaker, because recording calls lets a test pass without checking the returned data

options.misconception: believes a mock includes the stub behaviour and so proves at least as much

options.text: The stub test is stronger, because a fixed answer leaves the caller free to be written any way at all
options.misconception: believes a test that ignores how a value was obtained is the stronger check

It proves the wiring precisely, and it costs nothing, because a test may change as the code changes

options.text: It proves the wiring and the storage result, because the repository double still writes to the database
options.misconception: believes a recording double performs the write it stands in for

questions.topic: Boundary values and equivalence classes in the same function

questions.stem: A courier charges by weight in whole kilograms, free at 0 and over 30 kg, and a per kilogram rate in between, with express costing more. A team can afford eight test inputs. How should they be spent?

options.text: One input per class, the two class boundaries, and the last whole kilogram before the free limit
Eight different weights spread evenly between one and thirty, so the whole accepted range is sampled
options.misconception: believes uniform coverage of a range catches a boundary better than the boundaries do

options.text: One input per class only, because a value inside a class and a value on its edge behave the same way
options.misconception: believes a class has no internal edge where behaviour can change

A fresh copy of the original, because each test receives the fixture as it was declared at the top

questions.learningObjective: set a threshold that a performance regression must cross to fail a build
questions.stem: A rendering path has a measured ninety fifth percentile of 180 ms, and the same path measured across the last thirty builds has ranged from 150 to 240 ms. A proposal is to fail any build whose ninety fifth percentile rises by more than five percent over the last accepted value. What is wrong with the threshold?

options.text: It is far inside the run to run spread, so ordinary variation will fail builds and real regressions will hide in it
It is too generous, because five percent of 180 ms is a difference no user could ever notice
options.misconception: believes a small percentage change is always too small to matter

options.text: It compares against the last accepted value, so one accepted slow build makes every later build look fast
options.misconception: believes the baseline cannot itself be the outlier

options.text: It measures only the ninety fifth percentile, so a regression that moves the whole distribution is invisible
options.misconception: believes a tail percentile fails to respond when everything shifts

questions.explanation: The spread of 150 to 240 is about 60 percent of the median, so a five percent threshold sits far inside the noise: a build with nothing wrong will trip it often enough that the team learns to re-run, and once re-running is normal, a real twenty percent regression is treated the same way as a flake. A budget has to be set against the variation, and it is usually set with a comparison to a baseline measured the same way in the same conditions, repeated enough times to know its own spread. questions.hint: Compare the proposed threshold with the range the same measurement has already taken across thirty builds.

The tightened type check, because it rejects inputs that the unit tests hand over directly
options.misconception: believes a stricter input check is only visible to a unit test

options.text: The removed function, because nothing in the project calls it and only a full build notices
options.misconception: believes an unused function is detected only by running everything together

options.text: All three, because a version change alters behaviour everywhere at once regardless of the layer
options.misconception: believes a dependency's changes reach every layer of a suite equally

All three, because each is a measurement the release pipeline records for every build

options.text: The first only, since having a test per endpoint is the one claim the coverage report can confirm
options.misconception: believes the presence of a test is the same as the coverage of the endpoint

options.text: None, because a duration figure and a pass history say nothing about what was executed
options.misconception: believes timing and pass history are unrelated to the assurance question

questions.stem: A module exports a function that replaces its dependency with a cheap object, and a start-up path calls it so that a preview environment reports tidy numbers. Nothing in the code reads the environment. Why is this a production concern rather than a testing concern?

options.text: Because the substitution is reachable in production and no assertion anywhere in the product would notice the wrong result
Because a function used by tests should live in the test folder, so the build should move it out of the module
options.misconception: believes the problem is where the file sits rather than what it can do

options.text: Because preview numbers and real numbers must be produced by separate builds, and one build cannot do both
options.misconception: believes the same build cannot serve two environments correctly

options.text: Because the cheap object is slower in production, so preview and real runs would see different timings
options.misconception: believes a substituted dependency is a performance problem in production

questions.explanation: A test artefact is one whose reach is decided by something that is false in production, such as a flag the deployment sets differently or a file the build excludes. Here nothing decides anything, so the code path is live in every environment, and the result is a product that quietly reports a different number from the one it computed. The absence of a complaint is what makes it dangerous: there is no log line, no exception and no failing test, because the test suite is where the double belongs and it is the only place anyone looks. The repair is structural, by passing the dependency in rather than by remembering not to call the switch.

options.misconception: believes an empty input can produce a result of one element

options.text: The predicate mutates the list while filtering, so the result depends on the order of the calls
options.misconception: believes a mutation during filtering changes the element count

The suite has one assertion and no independent statement of what the answer should be, so it is checking that the code is consistent with itself, which is a much weaker property and one no defect can violate on its own. A refactor changes the signature of `find` from `(currency, country)` to `({ currency, country })` and updates the two call sites in production. The test fails. What went wrong, and what is the smallest change that fixes the test without weakening it?

options.text: The test asserted the call rather than the outcome, so restate the expectation against the new argument shape and keep the outcome assertion
The refactor changed behaviour, because a different argument shape can select a different rate, so the test was right to fail
options.misconception: believes an equivalent refactor can still change the value returned

options.text: The mock was too strict, so the fix is to make it accept any arguments and let the outcome assertion carry the test
options.misconception: believes dropping the argument check is the same as fixing the expectation

options.text: The test double should have been a stub, so replacing the mock with a stub removes the failure without touching the test
options.misconception: believes swapping a mock for a stub is the fix for a stale argument expectation

questions.explanation: The failure is the cost of asserting on a call: the argument shape is part of how the code is written rather than what it produces, so a refactor that preserves every result still breaks the test. questions.topic: A second test that inherits the first test's leftovers

The file passes. The second test fails when the runner executes the two in a different order, and passes when it runs them as declared. What is the actual defect?

options.text: The array is shared and never reset, so each test is asserting on a count that includes the other test's write
The runner is executing the file in an order the declarations do not describe, which is the fault to fix
options.misconception: believes a runner's order is a defect the test author must accommodate

options.text: The second assertion is wrong, because two records should give a length of two after both tests have run
options.misconception: believes the count of a shared array should include records made by other tests

options.text: The first test is wrong, because asserting an exact length of a growing array is never a valid check
options.misconception: believes a length assertion is invalid on any array a test may add to

questions.explanation: One array is created when the file loads and both tests write into it, so the second assertion is really asserting on one plus however much the first test left behind, and it happens to hold only in the order that was declared. Neither assertion is wrong on its own, and the runner is behaving normally: the defect is that the fixture is shared where the tests needed separate copies, which makes the result of each test a function of the others. questions.topic: A stub that answers so the real collaborator is never consulted

The real table has no entry for one of the three keys and returns nothing for it. Why does the suite stay green, and what does that reveal about where the assertion is pointed?

The real table is slow, so returning a fixed value is the only way to keep the test under a second
options.misconception: believes a substitute answer is required to meet a runtime budget

options.text: The assertion is correct but too narrow, so adding the other two items would have exposed the missing key
options.misconception: believes more items in the same test would reach the missing key

options.text: The lookup returns nothing rather than throwing, so the real table cannot signal the condition the test needed
options.misconception: believes a missing key is unrepresentable because no error is raised

questions.topic: A stored snapshot that fails on a reordering of the same data
questions.learningObjective: diagnose a snapshot failure that reports no behavioural change
questions.stem: A snapshot test stores `{"name":"ada","roles":["dev","ops"],"createdAt":"2024-01-01"}`. A refactor emits the same three fields and values in a different order. The build goes red, the reviewer looks at the diff, sees no value changed, and approves it. Six such approvals later the team stops reading them. What has the test become, and what is the narrow repair?

options.text: A ritual whose signal has decayed; compare structurally, or normalise key order and drop unasserted fields
A correct guard that caught an unintended change; the repair is to keep the stored text and pin the order in the code
options.misconception: believes a text snapshot is the only way to detect a reordering

options.text: A flaky test, since it failed on a change that was not a behaviour change, so the repair is to retry the comparison
options.misconception: believes a comparison that disagrees with the change is a flake

options.text: An ordering contract, since consumers may depend on the field order in the rendered output
options.misconception: believes the order fields are emitted in is part of the output contract

questions.explanation: Each approval teaches the reviewer that a red snapshot is noise, and once that has been learned a real change to a rendered value is approved in the same breath, so the cost of the text comparison is paid back as a missed defect. The narrow repair is not to stop taking snapshots, which is genuinely useful for large outputs, but to make the comparison structural or to normalise what nobody is asserting on: sort the keys, fix the order of any list whose order is not part of the contract, and drop fields the test does not claim to check. A snapshot that changes for a stated reason is evidence, and one that changes for an unstated one is noise.
questions.hint: Ask what the reviewer learned from six consecutive red builds that described no change in behaviour.

questions.stem: A rule bans any line containing the name of a retired function. Five lines are flagged: a real call, a commented-out call left in place during a migration, a registration of the function in a table, a string constant holding the name, and one real call made through a local alias. What is the cost of this rule, and what change keeps its value?

options.text: Two of the five are not uses and one real use is invisible, so the rule needs to read syntax and an allow list
All five are genuine mentions, so the rule is working and the migration is simply incomplete
options.misconception: believes a mention in a comment or a string is a use of the function

options.text: The rule is too narrow because it matches by name, so the fix is to match on the calling convention instead
options.misconception: believes the problem is which lines match rather than what matching means

options.text: The rule is fine, and the cost is only the reviewer time, so the fix is to batch the findings into one report
options.misconception: believes a blocking rule with wrong findings is only a time cost

It fails, because returning an empty list makes the handler throw when the body is serialised

options.misconception: believes the absence of an exception is the complete contract of a handler

options.text: It fails, because the runner compares the handler's output against the previous run's output by default

Add a log line inside the hook, deploy, and read the logs to confirm the hook is being called

options.misconception: believes one environment can be configured to avoid a code path it cannot see

options.misconception: believes a range check on the output is a substitute for fixing the source of the wrong value

questions.subject: WEB_DEVELOPMENT
questions.topic: An intermittent failure rate and the change that removes its cause
questions.learningObjective: compute an expected intermittent failure count and identify the fix
questions.stem: A test asserts that a value sampled from a three element list is less than three, and it fails on some runs only. The recorded rate is 33.3 percent. The build runs the suite 300 times a week. First give roughly how many of those 300 runs fail, then say which change removes the cause rather than the symptom.

options.text: About 100 runs, and assert a property of the sample rather than one draw, so no single value can fail the test
About 150 runs, and re-run any failure, because the code is correct and only the machine is slow
options.misconception: believes an intermittent failure is a timing problem the machine causes

options.text: About 100 runs, and seed the generator from the recorded time, so the same draw is produced on every run
options.misconception: believes fixing the seed removes the dependence on chance

options.text: About 10 runs, and raise the assertion to less than four, which every draw satisfies by construction
options.misconception: believes a wider bound removes a failure caused by a bound

questions.explanation: A third of 300 runs is 100, so a team sees roughly a hundred red builds a week, and at that rate a red build stops being information. Changing the seed makes a given run reproduce, which is what you need once a failure is in front of you, but it does not remove the chance that a run fails, so it treats the symptom and leaves the hundred. Asserting something true of every draw, for example that the result is one of the members of the list, keeps the check and removes the flakiness, which is the only version of this fix that reduces the count.
questions.hint: Multiply the rate by the number of runs, then ask which change makes every possible draw acceptable.

questions.subject: WEB_DEVELOPMENT
questions.topic: A file of five tests and how much of it can fail
questions.learningObjective: count the tests that can fail and interpret the rest of the file
questions.practice: auditing a file for failing power
questions.stem: A file declares five tests. Two assert that a computed value equals a written expectation. One asserts that a returned value is one of a set of allowed values. Two call a function and keep the result in an unused variable. First give how many of the five can fail, then say what the other two contribute to the file.

options.text: Three, and they contribute execution and a canary against a thrown error, but no check of a result
Five, because a declared test contributes a result to the report whatever it contains
options.misconception: believes a declaration is itself a check

options.text: Two, because a membership check cannot fail when the value came from the same list it is compared against
options.misconception: believes comparing a value against its own source list cannot fail

options.text: Three, and the other two raise the coverage figure, which is the reason to keep them in the file
options.misconception: believes coverage is the reason to keep a test that checks nothing

questions.explanation: Three of the five compare a value against something written down, so those three can fail and the other two cannot fail for any reason at all. What the two still do is real but small: they execute code, so a throw inside it fails the run, and they add lines to the coverage report. That is worth having as a cheap canary and worth nothing as a check, which is why a coverage number that counts them overstates what the file verifies. The distinction to carry into a review is between a test that can be wrong and a test that merely ran.
questions.hint: Count the tests that compare a value with something, then say what remains for the ones that do not.

questions.subject: WEB_DEVELOPMENT
questions.topic: Why a passing suite can still be inadequate
questions.learningObjective: explain how a green suite can coexist with an untested behaviour
questions.stem: A service reports ninety four percent line coverage, every statement is reached by at least one test, and the build has been green for six weeks. The team intends to state in a release note that the checkout path is adequately tested. Explain why the evidence does not support that sentence, and what evidence would.

answer.exemplar: All three pieces of evidence describe execution rather than detection, and the sentence is a claim about detection. Ninety four percent line coverage says that eleven of every hundred lines were never run, and more importantly says nothing about the ninety four that were: a line can be executed by a test that compares its result with a value derived from the same expression that produced it, and such a test passes when the code is wrong. A statement reached by a test that asserts nothing contributes the same line to the figure and none of the assurance. Six weeks of green builds is compatible with a suite in which no assertion can fail, because a green build is what a suite with no discriminating power produces by construction. The sentence would be supported by evidence of three kinds. First, a list of the behaviours the checkout path is supposed to have, with a named test for each, so the claim is about a set rather than about a percentage. Second, a mutation run over the path, with the surviving mutants named and each one either fixed or accepted with a reason, which turns an average into a list of known gaps. Third, a small set of deliberately broken versions, each failing the suite for the reason claimed, because a suite that has never been shown to fail has not been shown to detect anything. The honest version of the release note names the behaviours under test and the ones not yet covered, and the coverage percentage appears as a description of the files rather than as evidence of the claim.

questions.explanation: A model answer has to say that all three figures measure execution rather than detection, give the specific way a covered line can still be unchecked, and name the kinds of evidence that would support the sentence. Merely pointing out that coverage is an imperfect measure misses the point, which is that the sentence makes a claim of a different kind from the evidence offered.
questions.hint: Ask what each of the three figures would report if every assertion in the suite compared a value with itself.

questions.subject: WEB_DEVELOPMENT
questions.topic: Why a snapshot test is cheap and brittle at the same time
questions.learningObjective: explain the bargain a snapshot test makes and how to improve it
questions.stem: A team stores the rendered text of a large component and compares it on every change. Writing the test took an hour and it has caught two real defects. It also fails on most pull requests, and reviewers have started approving the red builds without reading the diff. Explain what the test is doing for the team and what it has stopped doing.

answer.exemplar: The bargain is that the test is cheap to write and expensive to trust. Writing it by hand for a large component would mean transcribing a hundred lines of expected output, which is why nobody does it, so storing the current output and comparing against it captures a great deal for very little effort, and the two defects it caught are real evidence that it works. What it has stopped doing is informing anybody. A comparison of text fails on any difference in the characters, so a refactor that reorders two keys, or a change to an unrelated field of the data, or a new field added for a different reason, all produce a red build whose diff contains nothing a reviewer needs to judge. Once roughly every pull request is red for a reason nobody can act on, the reviewer's approval becomes a reflex, and the test is now measuring how often the output text changed rather than whether it is right. The count of two caught defects is the honest measure of what it is still worth, and it is not nothing. The repair is narrow rather than abandoning the technique: compare structurally instead of textually, or normalise before storing, sorting object keys, fixing the order of any list whose order is not part of the contract, and dropping fields the test does not claim to check. What should not be done is switching the comparison off, since the cost that made the test attractive was the writing, and a structural comparison keeps that advantage while restoring the signal.

questions.explanation: A model answer has to give both sides of the bargain, explain why a text comparison fails on a reordering that changes no value, and connect the habit of approving red builds to the loss of the test's value. Saying only that snapshots are brittle misses the part that matters, which is that the cost is paid in reviewer attention rather than in machine time.
questions.hint: Consider what a diff shows for a refactor that changes no value, and what a reviewer does on the tenth such diff.

questions.subject: WEB_DEVELOPMENT
questions.topic: Why only a few journeys deserve an end to end test
questions.learningObjective: explain how to choose which journeys to test end to end
questions.stem: A team has budget for four end to end tests and a checkout path with nine steps, each of which already has unit and integration coverage. Explain how to choose the four, and what the team gives up by not covering the other five steps end to end.

answer.exemplar: The budget should go to the journeys where the pieces could be joined wrongly, not to the steps that are hardest to unit test. A step whose logic is already pinned by a unit test and whose agreement with its neighbour is pinned by an integration test does not become safer because a browser clicked through it; what a browser adds is coverage of the wiring that no lower layer can see, such as the order in which two services are called, the identity the session carries across a redirect, the value that survives being written to storage and read back, and the shape of the response a client actually parses. So the four tests should each be a complete journey that a customer would describe as one thing, and they should be chosen so that between them they cross every boundary on the path and every failure mode that has caused an incident. The team gives up two things and should say so. It gives up the reassurance that each individual step works in a running system, which is a real loss and is why the lower layers must stay strong rather than be replaced. And it gives up early detection of a break in an unchosen step, which will be found by an integration test, by a monitoring alert, or by a customer, in that order. A useful discipline is to write down, for each untested step, which of those three will find its failure; a step whose breakage would be silent and slow is a step that has earned its place in the four.

questions.explanation: A model answer has to argue for whole journeys over individual steps, name the wiring that only a full path can observe, and state what is lost for the untested steps. Merely calling end to end tests expensive misses the point, which is that the budget is better spent on boundaries than on steps already covered below.
questions.hint: Ask what a browser can observe that a unit test and an integration test between them cannot.

questions.subject: WEB_DEVELOPMENT
questions.topic: Why more of the same tests cannot raise what matters
questions.learningObjective: explain why repeating a test shape does not improve assurance
questions.stem: A team adds forty tests over a month. The coverage figure rises from 91 to 96 percent and two defects reach production, both in code that had been covered for a year. Explain why the campaign could have produced this result, and what the next month should contain instead.

answer.exemplar: The figure measures how much code ran, and the campaign added tests that ran code without asking anything new of it. Forty tests written to raise a percentage are, in practice, forty variations on the inputs already in the file, because that is the cheapest way to make new lines execute: one more value for a branch that was already taken, one more object of a shape the parser already accepted. Each of them is a legitimate test and none of them is a new question, so the figure climbs while the set of things the suite can contradict stays exactly where it was. That is consistent with both defects arriving from covered code, and it is the more uncomfortable reading of the month, because the number went up and the assurance did not. The next month should contain evidence rather than volume. Write the behaviours the module is supposed to have, mark which have a test that would fail if the behaviour broke, and treat the unmarked ones as the work list. Then check the marked ones against a mutation run, because a test that exists and a test that discriminates are different claims, and a surviving mutant is a request for a specific case rather than for another variation. Finally, look for the shapes of defect the file has never been asked about at all: an input nobody thought to try, a boundary nobody wrote down, a failure from a dependency, an empty result, a very large value. Those are where the two defects came from, and no amount of the same test will reach them.

questions.explanation: A model answer has to explain that the figure measures execution rather than detection, say why the campaign's tests could all be legitimate and still add no new question, and propose a work list derived from behaviours and from mutation survivors. Merely saying the team should write better tests misses the diagnosis, which is that the number rose for a reason unrelated to the assurance being claimed.
questions.hint: Ask what a test added to raise a percentage usually varies, and what it leaves unasked.

questions.subject: WEB_DEVELOPMENT
questions.topic: Ordering the test layers by what each run costs
questions.learningObjective: order the test layers by cost per run and by how narrowly they localise a failure
questions.stem: Put these five kinds of test in the order a team should reach for them, cheapest and most local first, most expensive and least local last.

options.text: A component test that renders one component with fixed props and checks the text produced
A unit test that calls one function with written inputs and checks the returned value
An end to end test that drives a browser through a purchase and checks the order row
A contract test that replays recorded payloads against a provider's current build
An integration test that runs a handler against a real store and a stubbed outside service

questions.explanation: The order runs from the test that can only be about one thing to the test that can only be about everything, and the cost rises with every step. A unit test needs nothing but the function, so it runs in milliseconds and a failure names a line. A component test adds a rendering environment and a few tens of milliseconds, and it can still name the output. An integration test adds a store, so it now fails for reasons outside the handler, which is what it is for. A contract test adds another team's build, so it fails for reasons outside this repository entirely, and it is worth its cost precisely because it is the only layer positioned to notice that the other side moved. The purchase test adds a browser and a payment provider, costs tens of seconds, and reports a missing order row whatever actually broke.
questions.hint: For each test, count what has to be running before it can make its assertion, and put the smallest requirement first.

questions.subject: WEB_DEVELOPMENT
questions.topic: Ordering the work that turns a generated failure into a filed case
questions.learningObjective: sequence the steps that reduce a generated failure to a small reproducible case
questions.stem: A generated case study has reported a failure with a recorded seed. Put these five steps in the order that turns it into a small case someone else can run.

options.text: Read the property that was violated and write down what the code claims about itself
Shrink the failing input by removing parts while the failure still reproduces
Replay the recorded seed to confirm the failure appears again on this machine
File the case with the seed, the shrunk input and the property, so it runs in CI
Find the smallest input that still fails and check the code path it takes by hand

questions.explanation: Replay comes first because everything after it depends on the failure being real on this machine, and a generated run can fail for reasons in the generator rather than in the code. Reading the property comes next, because shrinking without knowing what is being preserved produces a smaller input that fails for a different reason. Shrinking is the mechanical step and it is what turns a list of fifty prices into two, and it can only be trusted once the property is written down. Reading the surviving path by hand is what actually finds the defect, because a shrunk input is small enough to reason about rather than merely to rerun. Filing last is what stops the same input being found again, and carrying the seed with it is what makes the case runnable in CI by anyone.
questions.hint: Ask which step every later step depends on, and which step produces the thing the shrinking must preserve.

questions.subject: WEB_DEVELOPMENT
questions.topic: Ordering a benchmark measurement so the numbers can be compared
questions.learningObjective: sequence a benchmark measurement so two candidates can be compared
questions.stem: Put these five steps in the order that produces a benchmark result another engineer can act on.

options.text: Take the median of the runs and report it beside the range the runs covered
Fix the inputs, the machine and the settings, and write them into the report
Compare two candidates by the gap between their medians against the spread within each
Run the candidate repeatedly without recording anything, so caches and file systems warm up
Record every run rather than the fastest one, so the spread is visible

questions.explanation: The conditions come first, because a number without the inputs, the machine and the settings cannot be compared with anything, including a run of the same code tomorrow. The warm-up runs come next and their results are discarded, which is the step people skip and the reason first-run figures are always wrong: a candidate that pays for a cold cache, a lazily loaded module and an unoptimised code path looks slower than it is. Recording every run rather than the best one is what makes the next step possible, because a single figure carries no information about how noisy the measurement was. The median with the range beside it is the pair worth reporting, since the median resists the one slow run that a machine will always produce. The comparison comes last and is the step that decides anything, because a gap smaller than the spread is not a result.
questions.hint: Ask which step makes every later number interpretable, and which step can be skipped without anyone noticing immediately.

questions.subject: WEB_DEVELOPMENT
questions.topic: Ordering the response to a dependency upgrade that broke the build
questions.learningObjective: sequence the response to a build break caused by a version change
questions.stem: A dependency is upgraded by an automated update and the build goes red. Put these five steps in the order that gets the branch back to green with the upgrade kept if it can be.

options.text: Decide whether to adapt the code, pin the version and defer, or replace the library outright
Read the failing assertion and the trace, and write down what the code now does differently
Re-run the whole suite and the layers above it, since an adapted fix can break a caller elsewhere
Confirm the previous version is green, so the break is known to belong to the upgrade
Check the published changes for the library between the two versions, and match one to the difference

questions.explanation: Confirming the old version is green costs a minute and removes the possibility that the branch was already broken, which is the difference between investigating an upgrade and investigating something else. Reading the assertion before the release notes is deliberate: the failure tells you what the code now does, and the notes then tell you why, and starting with the notes sends you looking for a change that may not be the one that mattered. Matching one documented change to the observed difference is the step that turns a red build into a decision. The decision itself is the judgement, and pinning with a note is a legitimate outcome rather than a failure to upgrade. Re-running everything comes last because an adapted fix is a change to the code, and the layers that were not part of the original failure are exactly the ones that have not been checked yet.
questions.hint: Ask which step makes every later step trustworthy, and which one tells you what rather than why.
